source_type_decision.reason: The source wording asks for MySQL transaction isolation levels and the problems/boundaries they address. A concept/comparison answer is the narrow contract: define the four levels, compare visibility/snapshot/locking behavior on common dimensions, and state selection and engine/version boundaries without expanding into a standalone transaction-internals or system-design question.

primary_sources_checked.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual — Transaction Isolation Levels
verified_claims: InnoDB supports READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE and defaults to REPEATABLE READ.
REPEATABLE READ consistent reads reuse the snapshot established by the first consistent read in the transaction.
For REPEATABLE READ locking reads, UPDATE, and DELETE, a unique-index unique search locks only the matching index record, while other search conditions can use gap or next-key locks.
READ COMMITTED gives each consistent read a fresh snapshot and normally locks index records rather than gaps, except for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks; phantom-row problems may occur.
READ UNCOMMITTED may perform dirty reads, while SERIALIZABLE is stricter and converts plain SELECT to SELECT ... FOR SHARE when autocommit is disabled.

primary_sources_checked.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual — Consistent Nonlocking Reads
verified_claims: InnoDB consistent reads use multiversioning to present a point-in-time snapshot without setting locks on accessed records.
REPEATABLE READ reuses the transaction's first consistent-read snapshot, whereas READ COMMITTED uses a fresh snapshot for each consistent read.

primary_sources_checked.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual — SET TRANSACTION Statement
verified_claims: The default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ and the other permitted levels are READ COMMITTED, READ UNCOMMITTED, and SERIALIZABLE.
Transaction characteristics can be set with global, session, and next-transaction scope; session/global changes do not retroactively change an already-running transaction.

findings.message: The answer correctly distinguishes session-level changes from server defaults, but it does not mention MySQL's one-next-transaction isolation scope. This is not required by either source wording and does not affect the isolation-level comparison, so it is an optional precision improvement rather than a promotion blocker.
